title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Thanksgiving morning, Nov 26
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:20 AM ET Thursday, Nov 26, 2026 (Thanksgiving). Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). Abrego Garcia's departure is still the largest query (38,923 posts in 24 hours) but cooled overnight, about half the night before. The 'USAID Files' censorship story kept growing (27,274, up from 19,116 last evening) as Sen. Eric Schmitt pressed for a DOJ probe; the files' most-cited item is still an unfunded 2022 proposal. On the Far Left, the Fetterman–DSCC backlash rose (2,623, 19.33×) and widened into calls to replace DSCC chair Kirsten Gillibrand after an Intercept column, and the Van Hollen push climbed (10,533) ahead of the Dec. 1 vote as Sen.-elect Troy Jackson endorsed him. New on the Right: a month-old C-SPAN clip recast as 'Jeffries wants to bring back the illegals Trump deported' (942 posts, 5.65×); we found no plan or bill to do that. The Talarico 'stolen Texas' claim kept rising from a small base (2,031), while 'do not certify,' Newsom, DSA-LA and the Mamdani hotline cooled. One card was added and none dropped. U.S. trends were Thanksgiving and football; no card topic was on the list. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this morning or carried over from last evening and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 7:10 AM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). Thanksgiving and sports dominated: 'Happy Thanksgiving' (193,154 posts), 'Thankful' (134,373), 'Packers' (99,923), 'Good Thursday' (29,284) and 'Turkey Day' (12,397). Political or policy names: 'Trump Accounts' (7,342) and 'National Day of Mourning' (1,906); neither matched a card. 'USAID,' on the list last evening at 242,730 posts, was not on it this morning, so no card gets the trend bonus. 'Jordan' (130,109) and 'Golden' (166,997) were listed without context; we did not treat them as political. Where a trend object had no tweet_count ('Feliz Día de Acción de Gracias,' '#TheHuntingWives,' 'Bo Melton'), its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

Carried over from last evening: the fact-checks and outlets on the Abrego Garcia (PolitiFact, USA Today, Snopes), Talarico (Lead Stories, Texas Scorecard), USAID (DC News Line, Newsweek), 'do not certify,' audit, Newsom, Mamdani and DSA-LA cards. oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The new Jeffries card is tagged Right because it recasts an ambiguous answer as a promise by the incoming Speaker to return deportees. The Fetterman card stays Far Left; this morning the anger widened to DSCC chair Kirsten Gillibrand and feeds the push to replace Schumer. The Abrego Garcia card uses his departure to brand the Democrats who defended him. The USAID card casts a past Democratic administration's programs as a censorship operation. The Mamdani hotline and DSA-LA cards use city figures to brand the party. The Talarico, 'do not certify' and audit cards cast doubt on elections Democrats won. The Newsom card is the administration's attack on a Democratic governor. The Medicare for All and Van Hollen cards are pressure from the party's left on Democratic leaders. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Thursday, Nov 26, 2026, 7:20 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:10 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 25, 5:25 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. All eleven of its narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM ET Wednesday), so each card also reports its overnight count (5 PM Wednesday to 7 AM Thursday ET) against the same hours a night earlier. None was dropped: the lowest multiples were the audit card (0.68×, though its overnight count rose) and 'do not certify' (0.71×, still 16,929 posts). One card was added with a new query: the Jeffries deportation clip. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: calls to replace DSCC chair Kirsten Gillibrand (666 posts in 24 hours with a Gillibrand query, versus a prior daily average of about 6; folded into the Fetterman card), Republican attacks on Sen. Ruben Gallego's warning to Nvidia's board as a 'protection racket' (342 posts, 1.78×), and Trump's retelling of Putin's claim that mail-in voting makes U.S. elections unfair (76 posts, 0.46×, fading).

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Thursday, Nov 19, through 7:00 AM ET Thursday, Nov 26. The sum is the 'seven-day' total; the last 24 hours (7:00 AM ET Wednesday through 7:00 AM ET Thursday) are the 24-hour count; the last 14 hours give the overnight count, compared with hours 25–38 back. Daily bars are those hourly counts summed by UTC day. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official pages, court records, pollsters, transcripts, aggregators, X News summaries and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; this morning that includes a C-SPAN transcript. This morning we researched the new Jeffries card and updated the USAID, Medicare for All, Fetterman–DSCC and Van Hollen cards with new reporting; the other cards carry last evening's research and outlet counts and say so. No card topic was on the U.S. trends list.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list when we pulled it. The Abrego Garcia, USAID, Fetterman, Talarico and Jeffries queries had small baselines before this week, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out. The volume ceiling this morning is 38,923 (the Abrego Garcia query), down from 49,831 last evening, which raises every other card's volume index. Read the post counts alongside the scores.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The Jeffries query requires Jeffries plus a deportation, 'bring back,' reverse or ICE term, so it also catches unrelated ICE posts, rebuttals and left criticism of Jeffries. The other queries are unchanged from last evening and carry the same caveats: the Abrego Garcia query catches news relays and his defenders; the USAID query catches rebuttals; the Mamdani query catches explainers and translations; the Talarico query catches 'flipped Texas blue' celebrations; the Fetterman query catches primary news; the DSA query catches unrelated posts about DSA and violence; the 'do not certify' query catches rebuttals and other countries' elections; the Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and unrelated 'M4A' uses; the Van Hollen query catches syndicated news. Replies are included. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled a fresh sample only for the new Jeffries card; the other cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Jeffries promised to bring back the illegal aliens Trump deported' overstates an ambiguous moment. In the C-SPAN transcript of the Oct. 16 Pinecrest stop, Jeffries answered a question about returning people deported to third countries by calling for 'dramatic change' in enforcement and saying Trump's 'violent mass deportation machine does not get a dime'; the viral posts rest on a nod. We found no bill, budget or published Democratic plan to return deportees (Independence Journal; CBS Miami); the 'reparations' add-on in replies has no source. 'Gillibrand is stepping down from the DSCC' is not so: she has said she will seek another term, and the next Senate Democratic leader will name the chair after the Dec. 1 vote (The Hill; The Intercept argued she should be replaced). Carried over from last evening: 'Texas is being stolen' / 'apply the 0.85 algorithm and Paxton wins' has no evidence behind it. Texas's first statewide risk-limiting audit confirmed the Senate result with measured risk below 1% (Texas Scorecard); a federal judge dismissed the Potter County GOP's hand-count suit as 'speculation layered on speculation' (court order; San Antonio Current); and Paxton conceded on election night, so the circulating 'cannot accept' statement attributed to him is fabricated (Lead Stories). 'The DSCC endorsed Fetterman' is misleading: Gillibrand said the committee would back him in the general election if he wins the primary, and she did not endorse him in a primary (NBC News; Newsweek; The Philadelphia Inquirer). 'The USAID Files prove USAID got platforms to defund and deplatform outlets' goes beyond the documents: the most-cited item, a 2022 Global Disinformation Index concept note, is a proposal with no budget or award, and no public record shows USAID funded it (DC News Line); Newsweek said it is unclear which proposals were carried out. 'Mamdani is helping illegals evade ICE' describes a city legal-aid hotline that offers free immigration legal help; we found no rated fact-check, and the post itself does not urge anyone to evade enforcement (Townhall and LifeSiteNews quote it in full). Carried over from earlier snapshots: 'Abrego Garcia is an MS-13 gang member' is not supported; fact-checkers found the claim rested on a 2019 informant's account and his clothing, and that he had no criminal conviction (PolitiFact; USA Today; Snopes, 2025). '38 million invalid voters' is not a finding of illegal votes: the figure's own source, Unite4Freedom, describes the 38 million as 'registrations flagged for further investigation – not 38 million proven illegal registrations,' and we found no official finding that any state's result is in doubt (Democracy Docket; WOWT). 'Newsom is letting killers go free' is false: the commutations would change 548 death sentences to life without the possibility of parole, and none has taken effect pending the California Supreme Court (The National News Desk).

The busiest hour was 9 AM Wednesday (276 posts). Before Wednesday the query ran at about 70–215 posts a day. Democrat James Talarico beat Ken Paxton for Texas's U.S. Senate seat by about 1.2 million votes (55.1% to 43%), and Paxton conceded on election night (Lead Stories). Texas's first statewide risk-limiting audit, required by a 2021 Republican law, sampled 1,200 ballots from all 254 counties and found strong evidence the Senate result was correct, with measured risk below 1% against a 10% limit (Texas Scorecard). On Tuesday, Nov. 24, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kacsmaryk dismissed, without prejudice, a Potter County Republican Party suit seeking a statewide hand count of federal ballots, calling the hacking theory 'speculation layered on speculation' (court order; San Antonio Current; Houston Chronicle; KAMR MyHighPlains). County hand-count audits are still being posted. The new posts claim that applying a 0.85 'adjustment' to Democratic mail and early votes in Harris, Dallas and other counties would flip the race (X News); researcher Kate Starbird described this 'suspicious statistics' stage of election rumors after the midterms (Bluesky).
talkingPoints: Talarico got more mail-in and early votes than Paxton's entire total. That's impossible.
Apply the 0.85 adjustment and Paxton wins by a million.
A 1,200-ballot sample is not an audit. Hand count every ballot.
Cruz and Thune are treating a stolen seat as settled.
Texas has been Republican for 38 years. It didn't flip overnight.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @PoliticalStacy, @TheSCIF, replies aimed at Sen. Ted Cruz, and hand-count advocates such as Advancing Integrity (quoted by Texas Scorecard) and the Potter County Republican Party's lawsuit. Pushback: @dd19751981, @michaelandanneb and fact-check replies citing the audit.
narratives.whyItWorks: It turns a shock result into a math puzzle the reader can 'see' without checking anything: a big number that feels impossible and a formula that makes it go away. It fits a year of 'do not certify' posting and gives the base a single seat to focus on. And it lands on Cruz and Thune as much as on Democrats, so it travels inside the Right as a loyalty test.
narratives.audience: Texas Republicans stunned by the first Democratic Senate win since 1988; the national 'do not certify' audience; and MAGA voters angry at GOP Senate leaders.
narratives.counter: The state Republicans built the check, and the check passed: the risk-limiting audit Texas's GOP Legislature required confirmed the result, and a Trump-appointed judge threw out the hand-count suit as speculation. A uniform shift across counties is what a wave looks like, not a fingerprint of fraud; 2024 moved every state the other way. Paxton himself conceded. Ask anyone pushing '0.85' where it comes from and why it applies only to Democratic votes.

Jeffries has endorsed lowering the Medicare age and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits without naming an age (NBC News), and Axios reported Tuesday that lowering the eligibility age is harder than it sounds. talkingPoints: A buy-in at 50 is a half-measure — we were promised Medicare for All.
Rand Paul says $47 trillion; we say what does doing nothing cost?
Yale says Medicare for All saves $1 trillion and 114,000 lives a year. What are we waiting for?

Leadership and the 2028 hopefuls are out of excuses.

narratives.amplifiers: Left: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed), Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ('first phase' push, per X News), streamer Hasan Piker (via @socialistadri, 24,287 views), Common Dreams and Daily Kos. Aggregators: @Popstonox (372,266 views). Trump himself amplified the pitch on Truth Social. Opposition from parts of Trump's base in replies.
narratives.whyItWorks: It is a rare moment when the left's signature demand seems to have the president's blessing, so it turns an old wish into a test of the new Democratic majority: if Trump is open, any delay looks like leadership's choice. The gold-card gag is funny, visual and easy to share, and the left gets to troll Trump and pressure Jeffries and Schumer in the same post. Broad public support for guaranteed coverage in polls gives it a majority-sounding frame.
narratives.audience: Progressive and DSA-aligned voters, Sanders and El-Sayed supporters, young voters who follow streamers like Hasan Piker, and health-cost-stressed independents; Trump's base is the hostile audience in replies.
narratives.counter: Take the opening seriously and make Trump own it: ask him to back specific steps Democrats can pass in the first 100 days, such as restoring the ACA tax credits and lowering drug prices, and then build toward broader coverage. Be honest that a repost is not a bill and that a full single-payer system needs 60 Senate votes or a rules change. The win for Democrats is a health-cost vote Trump can't veto without breaking his own word.

factChecks.detail: Trump reposted a screenshot of El-Sayed's post with the 'TrumpCare' card on Truth Social on Nov. 21 after saying Democrats 'have some good points on healthcare' and that a bipartisan deal could produce 'great healthcare' (The Washington Times; Mediaite). We found no statement from Trump backing a specific Medicare for All bill or single-payer design. This is TDDR's read of the reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.query: ("do not certify" OR "don't certify" OR "dont certify" OR "withhold certification" OR "stop the certification" OR "38 million invalid") lang:en
narratives.sentiment: Insistent but recycled: the same Joe Hoft headline pasted into replies; a fringe 'storm the Capitol' reply; more 'show us the 38 million' and 'Joe made up the number' pushback
narratives.sentimentNote: Carried from the Nov 25 evening snapshot; we did not pull a fresh post sample for this card this morning. In a relevancy sample of posts from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Wednesday, the most-engaged post was '38 million invalid voters! There is no way in heck this election can be certified' (@Jessies_Too, 1,852 views, 328 likes). Much of the rest was one account pasting the same 'SERIOUS QUESTIONS ABOUT WHETHER US ELECTION SHOULD EVEN BE CERTIFIED: 38 MILLION INVALID VOTERS' line into replies to other users (@PatrJoe, at least eight times in about six minutes). One reply urged, 'Storm the Capitol to stop the certification of the results!' (@BCGrp_LLC, 33 views). Pushback grew: 'There aren't 38 million invalid votes' (@Edward_Morling), 'Joe made up the 38 million invalid voter number' (@seikjaboote) and 'Show us the facts behind 38 million invalid voters' (@dukelu78). This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: Morning update (Nov 26): 16,929 posts in the last 24 hours (7 AM ET Wednesday to 7 AM ET Thursday), 0.71 times the prior daily average of about 23,721 (last evening: 23,814 and 1.10×). From 5 PM ET Wednesday to 7 AM ET Thursday the query matched 6,924 posts, versus 13,801 in the same hours a night earlier. Still large but cooling: overnight volume about half the night before. We found no official finding that any state's result is in doubt. Last evening's card: Evening update (Nov 25): 23,814 posts in the last 24 hours, 1.10 times the prior daily average (this morning: 34,208 and 1.82×). From 7 AM to 5 PM ET Wednesday the query matched 10,011 posts, versus 20,398 in the same hours Tuesday. Cooling in daytime hours. It is still among the three largest queries, but the 7 AM–5 PM count is about half of Tuesday's, and the sample is dominated by recycled copies of Joe Hoft's Nov. 23 headline. No new official action backed the demand that we found today; in Texas, the state's first risk-limiting audit confirmed the Senate result and a federal judge dismissed a GOP suit seeking a statewide hand count (see the new Talarico card). We did not re-research news coverage for this card this evening, so its outlet count is carried over from this morning. This morning's card (Nov. 25, 7:25 AM ET): 34,208 posts in the last 24 hours, 1.82 times the prior daily average (last evening: 47,441 and 3.14×). From 5 PM ET Tuesday to 7 AM ET Wednesday the query matched 13,807 posts, versus 27,032 in the same hours a night earlier. Cooling overnight. New this morning: X News reported that Alaska certified its Nov. 3 results on Monday and Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan conceded to Democrat Mary Peltola, and that Ohio counties reversed course to count about 740 disputed provisional ballots. The query's daytime count Tuesday (20,401) was below Monday's same hours, and overnight posts fell by about half. The figure still has no official finding behind it; Unite4Freedom's own scorecard calls the 38.5 million 'unique registrations prohibited by law' across 35 states by its own analysis, not proven illegal votes (Unite4Freedom).
talkingPoints: 38 million invalid voters means no honest certification is possible.
There's no chain of custody for mail-in ballots and the machines were built for fraud.
Governors and secretaries of state must not certify until every vote is verified.
Trump should declare an emergency and audit all 50 states.
Democrats stole America.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: Joe Hoft (joehoft.com) and Unite4Freedom's Harry Haury; @jjauthor (the most-engaged post in our sample); Kari Lake ('Do not certify until you VERIFY the vote,' earlier this month); activists such as Kevin Sorbo, Gunther Eagleman and Scott Presler, whom X News named in the related push against Senate Republicans; and many small accounts quote-posting Hoft.
narratives.whyItWorks: A huge round number sounds like an audit finding, and the article borrows the language of federal law (NVRA, HAVA) and accounting ('material' errors). It hands disappointed voters one concrete demand with a deadline — don't certify — as states finish their canvasses this month. It joins the Michigan Wi-Fi and forensic-audit claims into one story, and the size of the Democratic wave makes a stolen election feel plausible to people who never saw it coming.
narratives.audience: Trump voters stunned by the landslide; election-integrity activists; Republican county and state officials facing certification deadlines; low-trust voters who read messy voter rolls as proof of illegal votes.
narratives.counter: Use their own source. Unite4Freedom says the 38 million are records 'flagged for further investigation,' not proven illegal registrations, and a voter roll with people who moved or died is not a ballot cast illegally. Certification is a legal duty, not a vote of confidence, and Iowa's Republican secretary of state defended his state's results. Point out who isn't buying it: Cleta Mitchell, Michael Flynn and Stop the Steal's Ali Alexander all said this landslide was real (Democracy Docket).
